title: Why messages get lost, duplicated, or reordered, and how to fix it
description: At-most-once, at-least-once, and "exactly-once" delivery. Why messages go missing or arrive twice, and how idempotency, dedup, sequence numbers, and per-key ordering handle it. The duplicate and dedup behavior was checked in Node, and the HTTP idempotency facts against RFC 9110.

questions.title: In an at-least-once system, why can the receiver get the same message twice even though the network never corrupts data?
questions.description: The bytes always arrive intact, yet duplicates still show up. Where do they come from?

images.alt: A sender and a receiver. The receiver gets and processes the message, but its acknowledgment is lost on the way back. The sender can't tell a lost message from a lost ack, so it has two options: retry or don't. Three lanes show what the receiver ends up with. At-most-once sends once and never retries, so the receiver holds 1, a gap marked lost, and 3. At-least-once retries until acked, so the receiver holds 1, 2, a highlighted duplicate 2, and 3. Exactly-once processing adds a dedup key at the receiver, so the second copy of 2 arrives and is ignored. A closing note states the Two Generals' Problem: over a lossy link, no finite exchange of messages makes both sides certain. Exactly-once semantics is the third lane and does not break that result.
images.caption: The middle lane: the ack is lost, so a second copy arrives.

options.text: The receiver's acknowledgment gets lost, the sender's retry timer fires, and it resends a message that already arrived.
TCP randomly reorders and duplicates application messages.
The receiver's buffer overflows and replays old messages.
It can't. Duplicates only happen with at-most-once delivery.

questions.explanation:
At-least-once means the sender keeps retrying until it gets an **acknowledgment**. The duplicate comes from a lost *ack*, not a lost *message*. The message arrives and gets processed, but the ack never makes it back. The sender times out and resends, and the receiver processes the same message again.

```js
const processed = [];
const receiver = (id) => processed.push(id);
receiver("m1");         // delivered + processed; ACK then lost
receiver("m1");         // sender resent after timeout
console.log(processed); // ["m1", "m1"]  ← double side effect
```

That's why at-least-once delivery always needs idempotent processing or dedup. TCP doesn't duplicate application messages, and receive buffers don't replay anything. The retry loop causes the duplicate.
questions.references: [Brave New Geek: You Cannot Have Exactly-Once Delivery](https://bravenewgeek.com/you-cannot-have-exactly-once-delivery/)

questions.title: Why do engineers call exactly-once *delivery* practically impossible, and what do real systems offer instead?
questions.description: If an acknowledgment might get lost, what can the sender do?

images.alt: A sender and a receiver. The receiver gets and processes the message, but its acknowledgment is lost on the way back. The sender can't tell a lost message from a lost ack, so it has two options: retry or don't. Three lanes show what the receiver ends up with. At-most-once sends once and never retries, so the receiver holds 1, a gap marked lost, and 3. At-least-once retries until acked, so the receiver holds 1, 2, a highlighted duplicate 2, and 3. Exactly-once processing adds a dedup key at the receiver, so the second copy of 2 arrives and is ignored. A closing note states the Two Generals' Problem: over a lossy link, no finite exchange of messages makes both sides certain. Exactly-once semantics is the third lane and does not break that result.
images.caption: Retry or don't. The sender has no third option.

options.text: Over a lossy channel you either retry and risk duplicates, or don't retry and risk loss. Systems pair at-least-once delivery with idempotent processing to get *effectively*-once results.
TCP already solves it by delivering every segment exactly once.
It needs specialized hardware that isn't widely deployed yet.
It works fine as long as every message carries a UUID.

questions.explanation:
When an ack can go missing, the sender has to choose: resend and maybe duplicate, or stay quiet and maybe lose the message. No protocol can guarantee both no loss and no duplicates. This is the practical side of the **Two Generals' Problem**. So real systems get exactly-once at the *processing* layer instead of the *delivery* layer. At-least-once delivery plus idempotent handling or dedup gives you **effectively-once**.

TCP does deliver each segment once within a single connection, but that doesn't cover application retries after a reconnect or a crash. The TCP option mixes up those two layers. A UUID alone changes nothing until you store it and check it, and that is the dedup step.

options.text: An idempotent operation has the same effect whether you apply it once or many times.

Idempotent processing turns at-least-once delivery into an effectively-once result.

questions.title: Messages on a single WebSocket connection arrive in the order they were sent. What most often breaks that order?
questions.description: The guarantee is real, but narrow. Where does it stop?

options.text: Spreading messages across several connections, consumers, or partitions. Order holds *within* one TCP stream, not *across* streams.
Nothing. A WebSocket server keeps a global order across every client connection.
Choosing binary frames instead of text frames.
Turning on `permessage-deflate` compression.

questions.explanation:
A single TCP connection delivers bytes in order, so one WebSocket or SSE stream is ordered for free. Once you fan out, that guarantee is gone. Two connections, several worker consumers, or multiple partitions can interleave in any order, because nothing coordinates them.

The usual fix is **per-key ordering**. Send every message that must stay in order, like all events for one user or document, through the *same* partition or connection. You get order per key instead of a global order. Frame type and compression don't affect ordering.

questions.title: A queue enforces strict total ordering, so each message waits until all earlier ones are handled. What's the built-in cost?
questions.description: What happens when one message in the middle gets stuck?

options.text: Head-of-line blocking: one slow or stuck message delays every message behind it.
Messages behind it are silently dropped to keep throughput up.
Acknowledgments can't be combined with ordering.
There is no cost. Strict ordering is free.

questions.explanation:
Strict total ordering costs throughput. If message #5 can't be processed because of a slow handler, a poison message, or a stalled consumer, then #6, #7, and the rest have to wait. That's **head-of-line (HOL) blocking**. HTTP/2 over TCP has the same problem: one lost packet stalls every multiplexed stream. HTTP/3 over QUIC was designed to avoid it.

The way out is to relax "total" to "per-key". Independent keys go through independent lanes or partitions, so a stuck message only blocks its own key. You give up a global order, which you rarely need, and get parallelism across keys.

questions.title: Which classic thought experiment shows that two parties can never be *certain* they agree over a lossy channel? It's the theoretical reason exactly-once delivery is impossible.
questions.description: Two words, about coordinating an attack. The full name ends in "Problem."

images.alt: A sender and a receiver. The receiver gets and processes the message, but its acknowledgment is lost on the way back. The sender can't tell a lost message from a lost ack, so it has two options: retry or don't. Three lanes show what the receiver ends up with. At-most-once sends once and never retries, so the receiver holds 1, a gap marked lost, and 3. At-least-once retries until acked, so the receiver holds 1, 2, a highlighted duplicate 2, and 3. Exactly-once processing adds a dedup key at the receiver, so the second copy of 2 arrives and is ignored. A closing note states the Two Generals' Problem: over a lossy link, no finite exchange of messages makes both sides certain. Exactly-once semantics is the third lane and does not break that result.
images.caption: It's named in the closing note.

questions.explanation:
The **Two Generals' Problem**, also called the Two Armies Problem. Two generals must agree on a time to attack, but any messenger crossing the valley might be captured. No finite number of acknowledgments makes *both* generals certain, because each new ack needs its own ack.

That's why message delivery can't be both loss-free and duplicate-free with certainty. You pick at-most-once or at-least-once, then build *effectively*-once on top with idempotency.

questions.title: A high-frequency telemetry feed can live with an occasional dropped reading, but duplicates would corrupt its counters. Which delivery guarantee fits best?
questions.description: Compare the cost of a lost message with the cost of a duplicate.

images.alt: A sender and a receiver. The receiver gets and processes the message, but its acknowledgment is lost on the way back. The sender can't tell a lost message from a lost ack, so it has two options: retry or don't. Three lanes show what the receiver ends up with. At-most-once sends once and never retries, so the receiver holds 1, a gap marked lost, and 3. At-least-once retries until acked, so the receiver holds 1, 2, a highlighted duplicate 2, and 3. Exactly-once processing adds a dedup key at the receiver, so the second copy of 2 arrives and is ignored. A closing note states the Two Generals' Problem: over a lossy link, no finite exchange of messages makes both sides certain. Exactly-once semantics is the third lane and does not break that result.
images.caption: The top lane accepts a gap so there's never a duplicate.

options.text: At-most-once. Don't retry, and accept rare loss so you never double-count.
At-least-once. Retry hard and rely on dedup to clean up later.
Exactly-once. It's the only acceptable choice for any metric.
Any of them. The guarantee makes no practical difference here.

questions.explanation:
Pick the guarantee by asking which failure is cheaper. For metrics, one missing sample barely moves an aggregate, but a duplicate inflates the counters. So **at-most-once** (fire-and-forget, no retries) is the usual choice. That's why StatsD sends metrics over UDP: it accepts some loss to avoid retries, duplicates, and backpressure on the app.

For commands, payments, and state changes it's the other way around. Losing one is unacceptable, so you use at-least-once plus idempotency. No guarantee is best everywhere. It depends on whether loss or duplication costs you more.
questions.references: [Etsy Code as Craft: Measure Anything, Measure Everything](https://www.etsy.com/codeascraft/measure-anything-measure-everything/)

questions.title: You dedup by remembering the ids you've already processed. What's the catch in practice?
questions.description: How much history can a real receiver keep?

images.alt: Five steps. A client sends POST /charges with Idempotency-Key: abc-123. The client generates the key itself, one per logical operation. The charge succeeds and the server stores the key with the response. The connection drops before the response arrives, so the client doesn't know whether the customer was charged. The client retries the identical request with the same key. The server finds the key and replays the stored response without charging again. A card lists what the stored record needs: the response, a request fingerprint so the same key with a different body is rejected, and an expiry, since after 24 hours the key counts as new. Six chips name the methods RFC 9110 defines as idempotent: GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS, and TRACE. POST is not among them.
images.caption: The record has an expiry, because nobody keeps keys forever.

options.text: You can't remember every id forever. Dedup only works within a bounded window, so a duplicate that arrives after the window can still get through.
You must store every id permanently, and then dedup is always perfect.
Deduping silently reorders the remaining messages.
Dedup only works on text frames, never binary.

questions.explanation:
Remembering ids costs memory, so real systems keep a **bounded dedup window**, either by time (ids seen in the last 24 hours) or by count. A retry that arrives *after* its id has left the window looks new and gets processed again. So dedup is a best-effort optimization. Operations that are idempotent by design, where reprocessing does no harm, are the reliable base.

Stripe keeps idempotency keys for 24 hours, and Amazon gives the same advice: pair a bounded key store with operations that are safe to repeat. Frame type has nothing to do with dedup.
questions.references: [Amazon Builders' Library: Making retries safe with idempotent APIs](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/making-retries-safe-with-idempotent-APIs/)

questions.title: Which techniques help a consumer keep or restore order in a real-time stream?
questions.description: Select every technique that helps with ordering.

options.text: Tag each message with an increasing sequence number so the consumer can spot gaps and reorder.
Partition by key so all messages for that key go through one ordered lane.
Buffer briefly to put out-of-order arrivals back in order before passing them on.
Send each message on a new connection to maximize parallelism.

questions.explanation:
Three of these work. **Sequence numbers** let a receiver notice "I have 5 and 7 but not 6" and wait or ask for a resend. **Per-key partitioning** (Kafka's model) keeps everything for one key on a single ordered log. A small **reorder buffer** fixes messages that race each other.

The false option does the opposite. Sending each message on a new connection throws away the single-stream order and maximizes interleaving. Parallelism and strict ordering conflict, and partitioning by key gives you some of each: order within a key, parallelism across keys.

questions.title: When a system advertises "exactly-once semantics" (for example, Kafka EOS), what does that actually mean?
questions.description: Does it break the impossibility results, or work around them?

images.alt: A sender and a receiver. The receiver gets and processes the message, but its acknowledgment is lost on the way back. The sender can't tell a lost message from a lost ack, so it has two options: retry or don't. Three lanes show what the receiver ends up with. At-most-once sends once and never retries, so the receiver holds 1, a gap marked lost, and 3. At-least-once retries until acked, so the receiver holds 1, 2, a highlighted duplicate 2, and 3. Exactly-once processing adds a dedup key at the receiver, so the second copy of 2 arrives and is ignored. A closing note states the Two Generals' Problem: over a lossy link, no finite exchange of messages makes both sides certain. Exactly-once semantics is the third lane and does not break that result.
images.caption: It's the green lane, not a fourth one.

options.text: Within its own boundary, it combines idempotent producers with transactional commits so each record affects state once. It doesn't extend to arbitrary external systems.
It physically sends each network packet exactly once.
It turns off retries so a message is never sent twice.
It proves the Two Generals' Problem wrong.

questions.explanation:
Kafka's exactly-once semantics is **effectively-once processing** built from two parts. The *idempotent producer* tags each message with a producer id and sequence number, so the broker drops retries. *Transactions* commit the write and the consumer offset together. Underneath, it's still at-least-once delivery plus dedup, which fits the impossibility results.

The catch: EOS only holds *inside* Kafka. Once a consumer triggers an external side effect, like charging a card or sending an email, you need idempotency at that boundary again.
questions.references: [Confluent: Exactly-Once Semantics Are Possible — Here's How Kafka Does It](https://www.confluent.io/blog/exactly-once-semantics-are-possible-heres-how-apache-kafka-does-it/)

questions.title: Per RFC 9110, how many HTTP methods are idempotent?
questions.description: Count the safe methods, plus PUT and DELETE. Answer with a single number.

images.alt: Five steps. A client sends POST /charges with Idempotency-Key: abc-123. The client generates the key itself, one per logical operation. The charge succeeds and the server stores the key with the response. The connection drops before the response arrives, so the client doesn't know whether the customer was charged. The client retries the identical request with the same key. The server finds the key and replays the stored response without charging again. A card lists what the stored record needs: the response, a request fingerprint so the same key with a different body is rejected, and an expiry, since after 24 hours the key counts as new. Six chips name the methods RFC 9110 defines as idempotent: GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS, and TRACE. POST is not among them.
images.caption: Six chips, and `POST` isn't one of them.

questions.explanation:
RFC 9110 defines **6** idempotent methods: the four *safe* ones (`GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, `TRACE`) plus `PUT` and `DELETE`. Sending any of them twice has the same effect on the server as sending it once, so a client can retry them after a timeout.

`POST` and `PATCH` are not idempotent. Retrying a `POST` might create a second resource or charge a card twice. That's why payment APIs ask for an `Idempotency-Key` header on `POST`: it adds idempotency to a method that doesn't have it.

```js
const idempotent = ["GET", "HEAD", "OPTIONS", "TRACE", "PUT", "DELETE"];
console.log(idempotent.length);           // 6
console.log(idempotent.includes("POST")); // false
```
